summary: Children move from comparing mass to quantifying it: expressing mass as a number of units — first non-standard (this book balances 5 cubes), then standard (grams, kilograms) — and reading a simple dial or scale. A balance shows equivalence (the object balances N identical units); reading a graduated scale means valuing the intervals, not counting marks. The key insight is that a larger unit gives a smaller count for the same object.
misconceptions: Uses non-identical units yet counts 'more units = heavier' (unit-size ignorance)
Reads a scale by counting marks rather than valuing intervals; misreads a pointer between graduations
Thinks the count itself is the mass regardless of which unit was used
Reads before the balance settles / uses a mix of unit sizes

activities.title: Balance it with identical units
steps: Place a book (or other object) on one pan of a balance.

Add identical unit-weights (e.g. interlocking cubes) one at a time to the other pan until the beam levels, or is as near level as you can get; if one more cube tips it the other way, the object is between two counts.

Wait for the beam to settle before reading, then count the cubes and record the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes', or 'about 8 cubes' / 'between 8 and 9 cubes' if it never quite levels.
Before you start adding cubes, check every cube is the same size; set aside any odd-sized ones.
Before adding any cubes, estimate how many you expect; after measuring, compare your estimate with the measured count.
activities.insight: Mass can be quantified as a number of identical units that balance the object; the record is a number plus a unit, not just a number.

activities.title: Same book, different unit size
steps: Measure the SAME book again, this time using larger unit-weights.
Count how many large units balance the book and compare with the earlier count of small units.
Say aloud why the number is different even though the book has not changed.
Discuss: can both counts be right at the same time — for example '5 big cubes' and '12 small cubes' for the same book? Explain how.
Place one large unit on one pan and add small units on the other until it balances, or is as close as possible — count about how many small units equal one large unit.
Answer: if you used really tiny units instead, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
activities.insight: A larger unit means fewer units are needed to balance the same object; the count changes because the unit changed, not because the mass changed. Conversely, smaller units give a larger count.

activities.title: Read the dial by valuing the intervals
steps: Look at a dial or kitchen scale marked at regular intervals (e.g. a mark every 100 g).
First work out what ONE interval is worth, e.g. the gap between two marks is 100 g.
Count the intervals (the spaces) from zero up to the pointer, not the marks, to find the mass — e.g. three intervals of 100 g means 300 g.
Read to the nearest graduation when the pointer falls between two marks.
Explain how you knew each mark meant 100 g and not 1 g.
activities.insight: A graduated scale is read like a number line: establish the value of one interval, then count intervals to the pointer — this is the same skill as reading a ruler.

activities.title: Compare and order masses from readings
steps: Weigh or read several objects and record each mass with its unit.
Decide which is heavier and which is lighter, and put the objects in order by mass.
Record comparisons using the symbols >, < and = (e.g. 300 g > 200 g).
Explain a comparison aloud, e.g. 'the red bag is heavier because 300 g is more than 200 g'.
activities.insight: Once masses are quantified in the same unit, objects can be compared and ordered numerically and recorded with comparison symbols.

checkQuestion: Give the child a balance, identical cubes, a set of larger cubes, a book, and a dial scale marked every 100 g. Watch how they work: (1) 'Use the balance and these cubes to find how many cubes this book weighs.' (2) 'Sam measured the same book with these bigger cubes and got a different number — why?' (3) 'Read the dial — what is the mass of this bag?'
checkAnswer: (1) Balances the book against identical, consistently-placed cubes and reports 'N cubes' with the unit. (2) Explains bigger cubes are heavier, so FEWER of them balance the same book — the count changed because the unit changed, not the book. (3) Values each interval (100 g) and counts intervals to the pointer, e.g. 300 g, rather than counting marks.
